newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA says fuel price limits profits rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA says fuel price limits profits rise.

text.p: British Airways Plc reported a 9.3 percent rise in first-half pretax profits to 470 million pounds ($769.6 million) on Tuesday, but said they could have been even higher were it not for the leap in fuel prices this year.

The airline said continued strong traffic growth and greater productivity would have boosted operating profits by 10.5 percent had it not been for an extra 51 million pounds on its fuel bill and the impact of a threatened pilots strike in July.

"The economic outlook for the main countries in which we operate remains generally encouraging with forecasts of continued steady growth in supply and demand," chairman Sir Colin Marshall said in his results statement.

In the event first-half operating profits were down by 2.1 percent on a year ago to 512 million pounds but the headline result was saved by a lower interest charge, backpayment of dividends on BA's $400 million investment in estranged U.S. partner USAir and an improved contribution by its 25 percent stake in Australian carrier Qantas.

BA's share price was unchanged at 549-1/2 ahead of an analysts' meeting. "The result is pretty much as expected with operating profit down and growth driven by non-operating items," said Guy Kekwick of Lehman Brothers.
Sales were up 9.1 percent at 4.4 billion pounds and operating costs increased 10.7 percent to 3.88 million pounds.
The dividend was increased 10.4 percent to 4.25 pence on earnings up 17.5 percent at 39.7 pence a share.

Chief executive Robert Ayling said the rise in oil prices along with some increase in flying pushed BA's fuel and oil costs up by a third so far this year and warned that further increases in air fares could be on the way.
"We have been whacked by our fuel and oil costs," he told Reuters in a post-results interview.
"It's for each individual airline of course to take their decisions on this but I think some of these costs we can expect to see coming out in increased fares in due course," he said.
"I think all the airlines have been taken by surprise. I would be surprised if you found many airline managers who guessed it correctly before Christmas last year. We didn't."

BA said it flew a record 20 million passengers in the half year with passenger traffic up 4.6 percent and sold an average of 75.2 percent of available seats per flight. This was down by 1.7 percentage points on a year ago but it had increased capacity by 6.8 percent in the same period.
BA said premium business class traffic remained strong, helping to push average fare yields up 4.1 percent in the six months to 6.54 pence per passanger for every kilometre flown.

Meanwhile Ayling said he remained as hopeful as ever that BA's proposed controversial link-up with American Airlines will be approved by the two governments but admitted the process was taking longer than expected.
"I remain more or less as optimistic as I was at the beginning (when the deal was announced in June)," he told Reuters.

BA and American have been waiting for nearly two months for British trade minister Ian Lang to decide whether or not to block the deal ever since his Office of Fair Trading (OFT) completed an investigation into the competition issues.

"The competition authorities here in Britain have approached it with a great deal of care and not rushed to judgement...So I am not complaining about the delay but it has taken longer than we originally thought." ($1=.6107 Pound)
